requirements.note: Newest first, grouped by day ('Today', 'Sun, Oct 25'), each header shows that day's total on the right; 240 seeded transactions.
Summary card shows October 2026 total ($5,269.70 on first launch) and expense count. It updates on add, edit and delete.

Amount on a decimal pad, merchant, category picker pushed in with all seven categories, date defaulting to today, optional note. Empty, -5 and three-decimal amounts are all refused with an alert. Swiping the sheet down with edits asks 'Discard changes?'.
Tapping a row opens a prefilled Edit sheet and saving updates the row. Swiping left shows the system Delete action, and deleting updates the day and month totals.
Categories tab: this month per category, largest first, with % share, count and a progress bar. Tapping one pushes that category's transactions for the month, grouped by day.
Amounts shown as $1,544.59. The add, edit and delete all survived relaunch.

bugs: One screenshot taken mid-fling showed torn text (the 'Sat, Oct 17' header and 'Water Util|ity' drawn split); it did not happen again in later flings.
tells: The month summary is a custom dark-green card with a multicolour segmented bar, a branded look rather than a system grouped list.
Save is a filled green capsule that is always enabled; bad input is reported by an alert after tapping, not by disabling Save.
In the form the date picker capsule floats centred under a 'Date' label instead of trailing on one row as in a system Form.
The calendar glyph on the summary card looks like a button but does nothing when tapped.
At the largest text size the row category icons and the card's calendar glyph stay tiny while the text around them grows huge.
Fun and Health both use near-identical red tints, so their bars and icons are hard to tell apart.
A.scroll: Slow drags, flings, flinging back to the top and pulling past the top all felt native, with no blank or popping rows, and scroll position survived a tab switch. The one exception was the single torn-text frame captured mid-fling.

requirements.note: Newest first, grouped by day; headers read 'Oct 25, 2026 · $222.02'.
Summary card shows the October total and expense count, and it updates live.

Grouped Form with amount, merchant, a menu Picker for the seven categories, a compact DatePicker defaulting to today, and a note. The checkmark Save stays disabled until the amount is above zero and a merchant is entered, with footer text 'Enter an amount greater than zero.'. 1.234 is accepted and silently rounded to $1.23.
Tap opens a prefilled Edit sheet and saving updates the row. Swipe-left shows the system Delete action, and deleting updates the totals.
Categories tab lists this month largest first with '% of this month’s spending' and a bar. Tapping one pushes its transactions with dates.
US currency throughout. The add, edit and delete all survived relaunch.

bugs: An amount with three decimals (1.234) is saved silently rounded to $1.23 instead of being refused.
Cancelling a half-filled New Expense sheet discards it without asking.
tells: No category icons or colour anywhere; the rows are plain text, so the lists look sparse next to a typical finance app.
Day headers repeat the year on every group ('Oct 24, 2026 · $87.47') and are set as grey list rows rather than standard section headers.
The category detail screen uses a small inline title while the other top-level screens use large titles; this is defensible but inconsistent.
The category bars are all the same system blue, so they carry no category identity.
B.scroll: Slow drags, flings, flinging back to the top and pulling past the top all felt native, with no blank or popping rows, and scroll position was kept across tab switches.

why: Both apps meet all six requirements and scroll equally well. B looks more like a stock SwiftUI Form, but it accepts three-decimal amounts and drops unsaved input without asking. A validates amounts strictly, protects unsaved edits, and has clearer category icons, colours and per-category counts, so it is the one I would rather ship despite its more branded, less stock look.
